title: AI agents meant to replace Meta workers made “large-scale, disruptive actions”
content:
Earlier this year, Meta created a “plan” to reduce some of its teams by as much as 60 percent to make the company “AI native,” Reuters reported today, citing two people familiar with Meta’s internal affairs.
Reuters’ report highlights the challenges organizations face when analyzing the best uses for AI and determining when the technology is a better fit for certain tasks than employees.
Meta confirmed to Reuters that the plan, reportedly codenamed Project OT (short for organization transformation), explored scenarios in which Meta reduced some team headcounts by 60 percent and that the plan called for two rounds of layoffs. Meta wouldn’t confirm which teams Project OT affected.
Meta told the publication:
As part of our company restructuring earlier this year, we asked some teams to conduct a scenario planning exercise looking at the potential impact of redeployments, open role closures and cuts. This ultimately resulted in moving thousands of employees to do priority work on several newly-established teams, as has been publicly reported. Ultimately, we didn’t move forward with every scenario from the exercise – and it was never assumed we would.
Reuters reported that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg “set Project OT in motion and directed executives to proceed with the changes to management structures” earlier this year. It said that the first round of layoffs from Project OT occurred in May and that Meta canceled the second.
Reuters said it reviewed “scores of internal documents, posts, and recordings” and spoke with “more than 20 people with knowledge of Meta’s inner workings” about the since-scrapped plans.
Per the publication, Meta executives created Project OT in January. Project OT reportedly explored using AI to perform “much of the daily work performed by thousands of human employees.” Small teams of people would oversee the AI, the report said, citing “one internal planning document reviewed by Reuters and three people familiar with the project.”

report.summary: Meta scrapped internal plans to cut 60% of some teams, relying on AI agents, after agents made disruptive workplace actions.
report.background: Meta's plan, codenamed Project OT, was part of CEO Mark Zuckerberg's push to make the company "AI native" by letting AI agents perform much of the daily work done by thousands of employees, with only small human teams overseeing them. Created in January, the plan explored cutting some team headcounts by up to 60 percent through two rounds of layoffs. Interviews with over 20 people and internal documents show that during testing, AI agents caused "large-scale, disruptive actions," prompting Meta to cancel the second round. The company eventually moved thousands of employees to newly established priority teams rather than dismissing them. The episode illustrates broader enterprise struggles: companies are trying to determine when AI is truly ready for autonomous work and where human judgment remains critical.
key_points: Meta's Project OT proposed replacing many routine jobs with AI agents, cutting some team sizes by up to 60 percent through two planned layoff rounds. The project began in January, but only the first round happened in May before the second was canceled.

AI agents reportedly made "large-scale, disruptive actions" during the exercise, revealing what can go wrong when autonomous systems are given broad control over daily workflows without enough safeguards and oversight.

Instead of broadly laying people off, Meta said it moved thousands of employees to newly formed priority teams. That suggests the company chose redeployment over aggressive headcount cuts once the AI risks became clear.

The Reuters report relied on internal documents, posts, recordings, and interviews with more than 20 insiders, giving unusual transparency into how Meta planned—and then backed away from—an ambitious AI-native restructuring.

For the wider industry, this is a key cautionary tale: even a company with deep AI resources found that replacing human workers with AI agents is less straightforward than expected, especially when agents must operate in complex, real-world environments.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this report reinforces the need for rigorous evaluation, observability, and guardrails before autonomous agents are deployed at scale. Developers should expect more demand for human-in-the-loop designs, rollback mechanisms, and fail-safe controls, rather than fully autonomous agent workflows. Meta's decision to redeploy employees instead of firing them suggests that the near-term future will be hybrid: AI handles routine assistance while humans supervise ambiguous or high-stakes tasks. Regular users can also take away that AI agents may be capable but not dependable enough to fully replace staff; workplaces will likely combine AI efficiency with human accountability, reducing the risk of harm but also slowing the pace of automation-driven layoffs.
report.tools: To follow up on AI agent reliability and oversight, watch observability and evaluation platforms like LangSmith and Langfuse for tracing agent behavior, and Arize Phoenix for LLM and agent monitoring. Open-source guardrail tools such as NeMo Guardrails or Guardrails AI are useful for constraining actions. These can help developers inspect agent decisions and avoid disruptive production incidents.
